newsitem.title: USA: Greenspan asks for panel to index benefits, taxes.
newsitem.headline: Greenspan asks for panel to index benefits, taxes.

text.p: Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan Thursday called for the creation of an independent commission to determine annual cost-of-living increases for federal benefit programmes and tax brackets.

Greenspan argued in testimony to the Senate Finance Committee that the Consumer Price Index, which is used as the basis for cost-of-living changes, overstates inflation by 0.5 to 1.5 percentage points a year.

The Fed chairman was one of the first -- and perhaps most influential -- of policy-makers who contend that the CPI is flawed and that the government is losing money by continuing to use it as an index for its programmes.
Millions of Americans, from retirees receiving Social Security benefits to taxpayers, would be affected by any change in the way the government calculates adjustments for inflation.
Greenspan argued that the creation of a national commission, which he first proposed two years ago, would not be the "political fix" that some critics charge.
According to the Fed chairman, leaving things as they are now would be tantamount to a political fix because of the widespread agreement that the CPI overstates the actual cost of living.

"There is almost a 100 percent probability that we are overcompensating the average Social Security recipient for increases in the cost-of-living, and almost a 100 percent probability that we are causing the inflation-adjusted burden of the income tax system to decline more rapidly than I presume the Congress intends," he said.
"On this issue, we should let evidence, not politics, drive policy," the Fed chief said.

He said the new commission he proposed could examine evidence on cost-of-living changes periodically and estimate the CPI's bias to provide a better calculation for the government. He suggested naming academics to the panel.
In urging action to alter cost-of-living adjustments, Greenspan added weight to the recommendations of a panel named by the Senate Finance Committee.

The panel, led by Stanford University economist Michael Boskin, concluded in December that the CPI overstated inflation by 1.1 percentage points. It said the problem was costing the government billions of dollars and should be addressed by Congress and President Clinton.

At the hearing Thursday and at one earlier this week where the Boskin group appeared, many members of the Senate Finance Committee -- including both Republicans and Democrats -- appeared sympathetic to the idea of changing the cost-of-living adjustments.
Yet many observers believe it might be tough to gain approval from a majority of lawmakers and from the president, given the controversy the subject has generated.
Advocates for the elderly and other critics have called the Boskin group's suggestions a "back door" attempt to slash benefits and raise taxes in order to trim the budget.

Besides calling for the creation of a national commission, Greenspan also backed increased funding for the Labour Department's Bureau of Labour Statistics (BLS) so that it could further improve the CPI to make it more accurate.
Greenspan said the bureau should first tackle problems that can be addressed quickly, within the next year.

At a separate hearing Thursday, the bureau's commissioner, Katharine Abraham, made a plea to the Senate Budget Committee for more money, which she said the agency could use to both improve the existing CPI and look at other potential cost-of-living measures.
Greenspan said a standing commission will be needed to determine cost-of-living changes, in part because many of the problems with the CPI may be difficult to fix.
"Even if the BLS moves aggressively, some upward bias will almost surely remain in the CPI, at least for the next several years," he said.
